articles.title: The Oil Market Is Brimming With Crude Despite Tanker Attacks
articles.summary: More than eight months into the Iran war, smoke continues to billow from oil tankers as Tehran presses ahead with repeated attacks near the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- More than eight months into the Iran war, smoke continues to billow from oil tankers as Tehran presses ahead with repeated attacks near the Strait of Hormuz.

And yet there's more than enough crude on the global market.

Saudi Arabia, the de facto leader of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, said it pumped 10.5 million barrels a day in October, a level reached only once since 2022. Iraq and Kuwait also reported big increases, while the United Arab Emirates is now free of OPEC quotas, allowing it to pump as much as it wants. Gulf shipments nudged lower this week, but remain healthy despite a slew of attacks, according to TankerTrackers.com Inc.

The ample supply has added to pressure on oil prices. Futures at one point this week were down almost 25% for the month, easing inflation concerns and offering respite for the global economy. Prices for physical cargoes have also plummeted, as producers compete for customers and exorbitant shipping costs begin to thaw.

The recovery is still precarious. Attacks have killed at least one seafarer this month and spilled oil is washing ashore on the region's beaches. With shipping under constant threat and Iranian media claiming attacks on navigational equipment near Hormuz, oil flows are erratic and could slow at any moment.

But Emirati officials at a recent conference in Abu Dhabi were keen to stress the resilience of the industry. That ability to keep crude flowing, mirrored across the Gulf, has helped bring Middle East shipments back toward pre-war levels and pushed Brent crude prices below $90 a barrel at one point this week.

"For us national shipping companies, there is no choice," Khalid Alhammad, president of ship management for Saudi vessel owner Bahri, said at a conference in Dubai. "We still have to go through the Strait of Hormuz. We have to keep moving the energy."

It's a remarkable turnaround from some of the worst fears at the outset of the war. Before the conflict, about a fifth of the world's oil flowed through Hormuz, and analysts warned that a closure could send crude prices above $200 a barrel.

Last week at Adipec, the Middle East's biggest oil conference, senior executives agreed that crude markets look well supplied heading into 2027, with further price declines potentially easing the fight against inflation, though efforts to rebuild stockpiles depleted during the war could limit how far they fall.

articles.summary: Wall Street's recent losses may not spell trouble for long, with Goldman Sachs seeing room for a fresh rally in the coming months.
articles.body: Wall Street's recent losses may not spell trouble for long, with Goldman Sachs seeing room for a fresh rally in the coming months. The brokerage expects the benchmark S&P 500 to reach 8,700 points over the next 12 months, as lower stock valuations could help markets gain ground despite a slowdown in corporate earnings growth.The target implies an upside of more than 14% from the index's last closing level of 7,592.40 points. According to Goldman Sachs, the recent market correction has made stocks more attractively valued, creating room for equities to deliver positive returns.The forecast follows a sharp selloff in shares of some of the biggest technology companies. The decline came after the Democratic victory in last week's US midterm elections fuelled concerns about a possible slowdown in data centre expansion.Goldman Sachs, however, expects the market to keep moving higher despite the possibility of slower growth. The brokerage estimates that earnings growth across global markets could at least halve in 2027. In the US, the pace could drop to 11% from 36%, possibly as hyperscalers ease the pace of their capital expenditure growth.This could put pressure on earnings across the AI infrastructure sector, where spending has been a key factor. But Goldman Sachs believes lower valuations, continued economic and earnings growth, softer bond yields and easing inflation could help equities stay in positive territory next year.The S&P 500 is currently trading at around 18.5 times its 12-month forward earnings, considerably lower than its recent highs of more than 23 times, the brokerage said.Goldman Sachs has retained its 'overweight' rating on US and Japanese equities, indicating a preference for these markets. It has maintained a 'neutral' stance on Asia and emerging markets, while keeping Europe at 'underweight'."From here, we expect equities to generate positive returns, albeit with higher volatility than in recent years," Goldman Sachs said.Meanwhile, the AI trade has faced another round of uncertainty amid developments at chipmaker Nvidia. The company's long-time CEO Jensen Huang quit following reports of alleged extramarital affairs, adding to concerns surrounding the AI sector.Nvidia's valuation has also fallen sharply. articles.summary: Binance is working towards restoring withdrawal services across all its remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, following a security breach
articles.body: Binance is working towards restoring withdrawal services across all its remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, following a security breach that led to $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency being stolen from the exchange last month.The company said it had brought 87 networks back online this week as part of its phased efforts to resume withdrawals. It had begun reopening the service earlier this month after covering 95% of the tokens lost in the attack."This week, we reopened withdrawals for 87 networks. Binance's first account of the incident outlined a hacking operation involving several stages, which reportedly started in June before a series of security breaches led to the eventual theft.Responsibility for the attack has been a point of contention. Both the FBI and Binance have identified North Korea as being behind the breach, while Pyongyang has denied the allegations. Blockchain investigation firms have linked the incident to a North Korean hacking group called "TraderTraitor".The scale of the stolen assets has also drawn attention to the security risks surrounding digital currencies and the potential consequences for Binance. The exchange has committed to reimbursing customers in full.The incident was followed by a change in the company's senior finance team. Kaiser Ng, who had spent more than five years as Binance's finance chief, stepped down just over a week after the theft to pursue a new venture.Justin Yek, who took over the role, is a longtime finance executive and previously served as vice-president of finance at Airwallex.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Inflation is pushing consumers to trade down and hunt for value
articles.summary: A Bank of America Institute report found that while consumers are still spending as inflation stays high, they are seeking value in some categories.
articles.body:
Consumers are still shopping, but they're looking for value as inflation stays stubbornly high.

A Bank of America Institute report found this is especially the case for millennials.

Trading down is prevalent in apparel spending, unlike for travel.

As inflation remains elevated , spending habits have changed, especially for millennials.

"Consumers are still spending, and they're adapting to inflation, but adapting is not the same thing as escaping it," Taylor Bowley, an economist at the Bank of America Institute, told Business Insider. "They're still finding ways to stretch their budgets by trading down where they have those choices."

The Bank of America Institute created a spending tier composite using consumer spending data across four categories — apparel, dining, grocery, and travel — and the median incomes of shoppers at premium, standard, and value stores to examine changes in spending. The composite has been trending downward over the past few years, reflecting the most consumer trading down since 2021.

That means "more households are shifting spending to value tier merchants" rather than high-end establishments and experiences, the new Bank of America Institute report said.

Affordability has been a hot topic this year. Gas prices have surged since the start of the Iran war. Mortgage rates have spiked since the start of the year, pushing homeownership out of reach for many. The Fed hiked interest rates in September to try to combat stubborn inflation but held rates steady in October as they seek more data.

Have you had to adjust your budget, dip into your savings, or take on another job as inflation remains elevated? We're looking to hear from people about their experience in the US economy. Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com .

Affordability concerns were also reflected in the University of Michigan's consumer surveys.

"About 57% spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices, the highest seen since May and up from 46% in February, just prior to the Iran conflict," survey director Joanne Hsu said in the latest release.

The bank's data showed trading down is more prevalent in apparel and dining. Travel, on the other hand, has seen an upward shift in the bank's spending tier metric.

Bowley said card data shows airline spending growth has been robust, but largely because of higher fares as transactions dip.

"There has recently been renewed strength in hotel spending growth as well as robust cruise spending — the latter often a budget-friendly way to travel," the report said. "Still, the increase in Bank of America's travel STC may reflect lower-budget travelers forgoing trips rather than becoming less price conscious given the decline in airline transactions growth in the past several months."

articles.title: Anthropic IPO draws six times demand, but valuation remains under scrutiny
articles.summary: Anthropic's IPO has drawn more institutional demand in its opening days than SpaceX's did, six times the shares on offer by Thursday.
articles.body: Anthropic's IPO has drawn more institutional demand in its opening days than SpaceX's did, six times the shares on offer by Thursday. Yet behind the rush lies a more difficult calculation: whether the Claude maker can justify a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.Demand for Anthropic's offering has outpaced the early response to Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO, according to people familiar with the two share sales cited by Reuters. The order book was twice oversubscribed by the end of Tuesday, the first day of Anthropic's investor roadshow, and had grown to six times the shares on offer by Thursday. SpaceX's IPO reached twofold oversubscription by the end of its second day of roadshow.The scale of the response is notable for an offering of this size. Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion through the sale of 825 million shares, priced between $70 and $78 apiece. At the upper end of the range, the company would be valued at about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis.The roadshow, which runs through Wednesday, has taken Anthropic and its bankers to prospective investors in New York, Boston and San Francisco. The company is expected to price its shares on Wednesday, ahead of their scheduled Nasdaq debut on November 19 under the ticker ANT.Yet the subscription figures tell only part of the story. Investors are being asked to place a price on a business whose revenue is expanding rapidly but whose position in the future AI market is far from settled.The challenge of staying aheadA central concern is whether Anthropic can hold its lead in developing advanced AI models as Google and other rivals accelerate their own efforts. Investors are also looking beyond Claude's popularity in coding to assess whether the chatbot can establish itself among knowledge workers across a wider range of industries.If several companies develop models of comparable quality, Anthropic could find it harder to maintain premium pricing. Investors are also divided over whether the AI market will ultimately be concentrated among a handful of dominant players or sustain several major competitors.There are questions, too, about how much clarity investors are getting before committing money. One investor who attended a roadshow meeting told Reuters that Anthropic had not provided detailed answers to some questions. Another investor said a group meeting did not include a conference call through which institutional investors could dial in and ask questions, as is customary in roadshows. Representatives of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley largely read prepared remarks at the meeting, the investor said.The biggest differences between investors are emerging in their estimates of how large Anthropic's business can become. Banks are using projected revenue of $270 billion to $280 billion in 2028 as a key input in their valuation models, according to people familiar with the projections.Sell-side estimates put revenue at about $52 billion to $53 billion in 2026, rising to between $135 billion and $137 billion in 2027. Some investors are more optimistic, with buy-side forecasts running 10% to 15% above those estimates for the two years, according to an investor who has placed an order in the IPO.Some investors are taking a more cautious approach with one investor who conducted due diligence but decided against participating has a 2028 revenue estimate about 30% below the sell-side projection.These differences are significant because the proposed valuation depends heavily on revenue that Anthropic has yet to generate. The company's current growth is striking: its run-rate revenue stood at roughly $81 billion on October 31, up from $71 billion a month earlier, according to its IPO filing. But investors must decide how much of that momentum can be sustained as competition intensifies.The valuation exercise is complicated by the lack of obvious comparisons. Investors are looking at companies including SpaceX and cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike as benchmarks, even though neither offers a direct comparison with an AI model developer.Growth comes with a huge infrastructure billAnthropic's expansion also depends on access to computing capacity on an extraordinary scale. Its IPO filing lists nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Google's parent Alphabet. Securing that capacity will be central to the company's ability to meet future demand, but it also underscores the scale of the resources required to sustain its growth.The wider AI sector is facing scrutiny over whether the money being poured into infrastructure will produce returns commensurate with the investment. A recent technology-stock selloff has added to concerns about spending, financing costs and the possibility that the industry may not deliver on the expectations built into current valuations.Anthropic is seeking a further $26 billion through a separate private placement with cornerstone investors including Alphabet, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Along with commitments from investors such as Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft and TSMC, the combined fundraising could reach $90.4 billion.The company was valued at $965 billion in a private funding round in May. Its IPO is therefore a major step up from its last private valuation, even as investors debate how much future success is already priced in.The listing is also being watched as a possible indicator of investor appetite for rival OpenAI, which is seeking to raise $30 billion in what is expected to be its final private funding round before a potential IPO early next year.Anthropic's early order book suggests that demand for large AI offerings remains robust. The more consequential test, however, will be whether investors remain convinced by the company's growth assumptions and competitive prospects when the final price is set.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang fallout: Here's everything we know after a momentous week
articles.summary: Here's a giant rundown of everything that happened with Nvidia this week.
articles.body:
The rapid-fire pace of the Nvidia ( NVDA ) scandal has left everyone a little disoriented. So we thought we'd make a giant rundown of what's happened — and what we've been thinking about to help make sense of the very fluid situation.

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned under pressure from the board. The one-two punch of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and then news of another one with an Nvidia executive (plus a third with an unnamed employee revealed Thursday afternoon) turned out to be too much for the company's board to ignore . Huang was among the longest-serving CEOs in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ), with a 33-year tenure.

CFO Nicole Kress is now the interim CEO. Kress has been at the company since 2013 and has been a mainstay on earnings calls as the financial head. She'll have an immediate test: The company will still report earnings next Tuesday, and markets want to know whether she'll continue Huang's "Bank of Nvidia" approach to circular dealmaking . That entire web is under the microscope now.

What this means for earnings? Not much, beyond all the questions Kress will have to answer. That quarter is over. But all eyes will be on the outlook and on whether Nvidia seems to have its act together.

Nvidia stock fell 4.3% the day Huang resigned. It initially fell as much as 14% on Thursday morning but recovered. It momentarily became the third-most-valuable company by market cap, behind Apple and Microsoft .

Context-wise, these are 2025 stock prices for NVDA. The stock is down 13% over the past five days, 25% in the past month (and the past six months), and 12% so far this year. And 14% from a year ago. The stock is essentially back to summer 2025 levels.

Retail investors bought the dip. A big part of why that double-digit loss became only 4.3%? People like you. As one analyst, Mike Zaccardi, put it on X, it was "one of the more epic 'buy the news' events in history."

Wall Street is lowering price targets. Yorkville Ives's Dan Ives, a prominent Nvidia bull, lowered his price target from $300 to $225, valuing Huang's leadership at a 25% premium. The longer-term outlook, broadly, seems clouded , but most analyst notes we've read say that Kress's knowledge of the business makes her seem like a steady pair of hands.

The CEO search is going to be critical. Already, speculation about who will be the new permanent CEO has reached fever pitch, with President Trump suggesting Tim Cook, "the only one man to take his place."

Prediction markets favor Ian Buck as long-term successor. Kalshi and Polymarket are giving Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing a 1-in-3 chance. Here's who he is. Still, that's not a high probability, and it could be anyone with electrical engineering prowess or heavy Big Tech experience — preferably with charisma.

articles.title: Is it smart to get an investment property?
articles.summary: Ask yourself a few critical questions before purchasing a rental property.
articles.body: Buying a rental property and becoming a landlord may be a good investment … or not. But either way, it’s a job. In this week’s Ask the Expert, which is part of CNN’s Savings Challenge, Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, offers a few questions to gauge whether the move would be right for you. Reader: Is an investment property worth it? DOUG: The honest answer? It depends! And anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Investment properties can absolutely build wealth over time. The combination of rental income, appreciation and tax advantages like depreciation has made real estate a meaningful part of a lot of people’s financial lives. I get why it’s appealing. But here’s what the highlight reels on social media tend to leave out. Owning rental property is a job. You are a landlord. That means tenants, vacancies, maintenance calls, repairs you didn’t budget for and the occasional nightmare scenario that no spreadsheet prepares you for. Before you pull the trigger, I’d want you to honestly answer a few questions. If the numbers work and you have the stomach for it, real estate can be a legitimate wealth-building tool. If you’re stretching to make it work on paper, it’s probably not worth it. Run the numbers (not just the optimistic ones) and let those be your guide. Tip of the week: Quick ways to up your credit score Credit scores help determine if you get approved for a loan – or an insurance policy. The higher your score, the lower your interest rate and monthly payments. Many factors go into a score, but one way to raise yours quickly is to lower the utilization rate on your credit cards. That’s the percentage your outstanding balances together represent relative to your combined credit limit. For example, if you have a combined limit of $30,000 across three credit cards and your balances add up to $15,000, your utilization rate is 50%. If you have a $5,000 combined balance, your rate drops to roughly 17%. Your utilization rate ideally should be below 30%. Here are some ways to improve it:

articles.title: ‘Separating wants and needs’: Milwaukee couple reconsider their financial habits
articles.summary: Being able to clear their credit card debts thanks to a modest inheritance was a gift for Mariza and Geffrey Gordon. But not a financial cure-all.
articles.body: Being able to clear their credit card debts thanks to a modest inheritance was a gift for Mariza and Geffrey Gordon. And it boosted their credit scores by more than 100 points to roughly 750. But that alone will not remedy their financial situation of living paycheck to paycheck and not having enough saved for emergencies. A more permanent fix will involve changing their money habits. Their Savings Challenge work with financial educator Tiffany Aliche has shown the Milwaukee-based couple some things they weren’t willing to look at previously. “The most difficult thing and probably one of the better things was it (forced us) to face (our) financial habits, bad, good or indifferent,” Geffrey said. “A lot of times in the past we’ve avoided facing our habits …. And this is something I can take moving forward, to just be willing to face it. There’s no way to improve if you don’t face it.” But improving may be a bumpy ride for the foreseeable future. On the one hand, the couple has started to regularly consider what is necessary to spend money on versus what they’d like to spend money on. “Separating wants and needs will be helpful for us moving forward,” Geffrey said. For example, they have cut back on spending for clothes, travel, concerts and sporting events, he said. And while they bought a garbage disposal to replace their broken one, he noted, they decided not to install it since it would have cost them money and they realized they can live without it for now. But they did go ahead with two other big home expenses. They installed new carpeting because the old carpet had a terrible smell even after cleaning it, Mariza explained. And they bought some furniture for their bedroom, which had been bare except for the bed itself, she said. They put down $400 cash for the furniture and put the rest on a 0% store card, which they qualified for after their credit scores jumped. Mariza said they are paying off the purchase monthly, noting that they expect to clear that debt well before their 0% rate expires. Tiffany said she would have advised that they not take on any debt unless it secures safety and health for them. The goal for now: Maintain rather than boost savings Mariza, who was laid off earlier this year from a job as a plan consultant at a financial services firm, hasn’t found a new position yet. Until she does, Tiffany told the couple to worry less about putting money away, and instead maintain the savings they have. But they said they are dipping into what remains of their inheritance and into the 20% of savings automatically set aside from Geffrey’s paycheck to pay Mariza’s $555 monthly car note and help cover general expenses. Still, Geffrey said he is glad he arranged for a direct deposit from his paycheck into savings, a setup that he expects to be more beneficial once his wife gets a job and they have two incomes again. At that point, he added, they plan to follow Tiffany’s advice to prioritize saving for emergencies. Their goal is having an emergency fund to cover them for six months in case either one loses a job again. Keeping perspective At this writing, Mariza said she has been going on interviews and did freelance work curating an art show featuring local artists. As for health insurance, she said she is resigned to not having it for now and plans to sign onto her husband’s plan for 2027 if she doesn’t have a job by then. In the meantime, to save on food and other goods, the couple said they will continue buying in bulk at Costco and plan to cook more meals at home. Throughout their Savings Challenge, which coincided with Mariza’s layoff, she said she has learned to be more mindful of her blessings and not take them for granted, especially when she feels discouraged on the job front. “Things could be so much worse,” she said. What’s next: Next week, we’ll share our final update on math and tennis teacher Jeff Kizer’s Savings Challenge work.

articles.title: CVS says GLP-1s save money when priced below $350 per month
articles.summary: NEW YORK, Nov 14 (Reuters) - CVS Health said employers and other health plan sponsors could break even on GLP-1 drugs if they are priced below $350 per month...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Nov 14 (Reuters) - CVS Health said employers and other health plan sponsors could break even on GLP-1 drugs if they are priced below $350 per month as reduced use of medical services, such as hospitalizations and ‌emergency room visits, lower spending enough to offset drug costs.

CVS said that an analysis of its Aetna insurance claims data found ‌that across patients with obesity, diabetes or other conditions, the current prices for GLP-1 drugs add to spending because they are too high to be impacted by lower ​medical costs.

The analysis looked at patients who were newly taking highly popular GLP-1 medicines — which mimic the GLP-1 hormone and reduce appetite — from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, and compared them to similar patients who were not taking the drugs.

The drugs included Mounjaro and Ozempic for diabetes and Zepbound and Wegovy for obesity. The analysis covered periods of up to three years, with patients starting the medicines between 2023 and 2025.

The analysis did not ‌break out figures for obesity patients alone.

Coverage of GLP-1 drugs for obesity is falling as corporations and other health plan sponsors try to bring down premiums expected to be up by over 9% in 2027. About 14% of companies have already ⁠dropped or plan to drop the drugs in 2027.

Zepbound and Wegovy can cost about $299 and $349 for cash-pay customers. Employers and other health plan sponsors pay between $617 and $766 monthly for the drugs, according to a 2025 study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute. CVS declined to comment on the average prices paid.

Dr ​Amy ​Compton-Phillips, chief medical officer at CVS Health, said that the drugmakers' direct-to-consumer prices ​suggest they can still profit by charging less than $350 ‌a month, while also helping to lower overall healthcare costs. The United States pays more for healthcare than any other country.

"I hope that we can reach that price sooner rather than later," she said in an interview ahead of the HLTH USA conference in Las Vegas, where CVS will present the findings on November 15.

The US government agreed on a deal with Lilly and Novo last year to pay $245 per month for injectable GLP-1 weight-loss drugs in an 18-month pilot testing their cost-effectiveness for Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 and older or with disabilities.

CVS said GLP-1 ‌use for obesity, diabetes or other conditions was associated with 10-12% lower emergency ​room visits in the first and second year of use. It examined records for ​60,000 people during the first year and 20,000 people for ​a second year.

articles.title: 'Will change the Tata way': Noel warns Tata Sons listing could put profits ahead of philanthropy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata on Saturday cautioned that a public listing of Tata Sons could change the Tata Group’s traditional business
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata on Saturday cautioned that a public listing of Tata Sons could change the Tata Group’s traditional business philosophy, warning that a larger shareholder base may eventually prioritise profits over philanthropy."My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way. And one day, if we have 30,000-40,000 shareholders, profit may take precedence over philanthropy. And I think that will fundamentally change the Tata way of working," Noel said while speaking at the HT Leadership Summit 2026."Tata Trusts will play a constructive role with regulators and others to try and find a solution which keeps the Tata way the way it is," he added.His remarks come amid an intensifying disagreement between Tata Trusts and the Tata Sons board over the holding company's ownership structure and leadership.Tata Trusts, which holds about 66% of Tata Sons, has opposed a public listing, PTI reported.The Shapoorji Pallonji Group, the second-largest shareholder with an 18.37% stake, has backed a stock market listing to unlock value from its investment.Speaking about the group's future priorities, Noel said he did not question its broad strategic direction but believed it needed greater discipline in executing large projects and allocating capital."Philanthropy on one hand. Nation building on the other. This is independence of leadership and personalities and this will continue. I do not question the direction of what we have done. I question, sometimes, the delivery of what we are doing," he said."The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction? How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don't have discipline? And how will we allocate capital to those projects?" he said, PTI reported."So, very clearly, the direction is fine, but we also need discipline in the execution of these very large projects," he added.Noel highlighted the group's participation in emerging sectors, including semiconductors and electric vehicle batteries, as part of its contribution to India's industrial development."We are partners in India's development," he said, adding that the group was undertaking its first semiconductor project and setting up its first EV battery plant.Noel also spoke about the growth of the group's retail business, particularly Trent, which operates the Westside and Zudio brands.He also said his work as chairman of Tata Trusts had given him a deeper understanding of the needs of underserved communities and made him more aware of the scale of India's social challenges.What is behind the Tata Sons listing dispute?The dispute gathered pace after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected Tata Sons' application in September 2026 to surrender its registration as a core investment company.The decision effectively closed a route the group had pursued to avoid mandatory listing as an upper-layer non-banking financial company. At a September 17 board meeting, Tata Sons decided to initiate steps towards a listing in line with RBI regulations.The board also approved a fresh five-year term for chairman N Chandrasekaran, reversing his August decision not to seek reappointment after February 2027.Noel opposed both decisions. Tata Trusts subsequently questioned the legality of Chandrasekaran's reappointment, which was approved by the board in a 4:1 vote.Reiterating the importance of continuity in the group's ownership structure, Noel said its institutional framework had helped preserve the Tata philosophy across generations."The owner cannot die, the owner cannot be bought and the owner cannot retire. There is continuity in what happens the Tata way," he said.The Tata Group has traditionally combined commercial operations with philanthropy and nation-building, with Tata Trusts playing a central role in its institutional structure.Why some trustees support a listingMeanwhile, Tata Trusts vice-chairman Venu Srinivasan and other trustees supporting a public listing are understood to favour greater transparency, stronger corporate governance and a clearer ownership structure for the conglomerate.They argue that a listing would bring Tata Sons under greater public and regulatory scrutiny, strengthen institutional decision-making and reduce uncertainty around succession and governance.It could also provide a market-determined valuation of the holding company and give investors greater visibility into the group's financial and strategic decisions, PTI reported.In a November 11 letter to fellow trustee Darius Khambata, Srinivasan and fellow vice-chairman Vijay Singh cited companies such as Novo Nordisk, Hershey, Lundbeck and Demant to argue that businesses can remain anchored by charitable foundations while being publicly traded.They also pointed to listed Tata companies, including TCS, Tata Steel, Tata Power and Tata Motors, which have undertaken long-term investments and nation-building projects while retaining their institutional character.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: The bond market just turned on the AI trade — and chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in two days: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Traders pricing in a Fed rate hike just took away the AI trade's bond market cushion.
articles.body:
Wall Street just had its best week since August, and chip stocks led the way. But by Friday the rally was cracking, and the bond market had turned against the AI trade.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) still finished the week up about 8%, with the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) up about 3.5% and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) up about 2.5%. Most of those gains came early. From Wednesday's close through Friday, a Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in market value, and only three rose.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) never joined the rally. The stock fell about 13% in the week Jensen Huang resigned as CEO , its worst week since April 2025 and its sixth straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2012. That wiped out about $570 billion in value as investors weighed Nvidia's $530 billion web of AI deals .

The damage spread to Nvidia's partners. Nebius ( NBIS ), in which Nvidia holds a stake, fell about 10% for the week after disappointing third quarter earnings . Nvidia-backed CoreWeave ( CRWV ) slid about 6% Friday, though it still finished up about 15% after strong quarterly results . Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ), leaders of the early-week bounce, gave back roughly 3% to 4% Friday.

The charts show where the rebound ran out of steam. The chip index stalled before it got back to its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line. The Nasdaq-100 closed back below its own similar average, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) closed right at it.

During the AI sell-off, Treasurys acted as a shock absorber. The 10-year yield ( ^TNX ) fell on all six of chip stocks' down days from Oct. 22 to Nov. 6, as investors bought bonds when chips sank.

But this past week, yields rose on all three days when semis were down. The 10-year jumped about 30 basis points to about 5.15%, and the 5-year climbed about 33 basis points. For both, it was the biggest weekly rise since April 2025.

Over the sell-off, every chip crash made traders doubt a hike was coming. Polymarket's odds of a Dec. 9 rate increase fell to about 66% after the Nov. 5 rout. By Friday, they were about 98%, with the odds of a half-point move up to 10%. Futures now price in about two quarter-point hikes by March 2027, up from one right after the crash.

articles.title: When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies?
articles.summary: Nvidia could lose 30 percent of its value following cofounder Jensen Huang’s decision to step down, analysts warns.
articles.body:
In the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia, the company has brought in a new interim chief, Colette Kress , who has been with the company since 2013.

Along with Kress, the AI bellwether appointed its first-ever board chair, Harvey Jones, a venture investor with three decades of tech industry experience.

The changes mark a major overhaul of Nvidia’s corporate structure and leadership, which Huang has dominated since cofounding the AI chipmaker in 1993. A powerful figure in Silicon Valley, he stepped down on Thursday following reports of his affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and two employees that have drawn scrutiny from United States lawmakers, the company’s board and shareholders.

Despite the shakeup, the question remains how much of Nvidia’s nearly $4 trillion value was pegged to its longtime leader, who is synonymous with the company’s exponential growth. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, predicted that Nvidia’s value could decline 25 to 30 percent without Huang at the helm.

Historically, executives across corporate America have been beholden to shareholders, who hold executives accountable. In Silicon Valley, however, companies have often been built around a founder’s vision – as was the case for Nvidia.

Why do tech companies put so much faith in their founders?

Analysts have long maintained that the success of companies like Nvidia hinges on the success and vision of their founder. A report from Bain and Company found that founder-led companies perform 2.1 times better than companies that are not led by their founders between 2015 and 2025, and when it comes to tech, that jumps to 2.6 times.

“When it comes to succession, the data shows that, as great as these founders are, it’s incredibly rare for their successors to do as well as the original founder. So I wouldn’t necessarily call it a risk. It’s simply the evolutionary life cycle of building a company,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.

Silicon Valley has long embraced this model, with companies such as Meta – Facebook and Instagram’s parent company – and Tesla built around the vision and personalities of their founders.

“It’s a common challenge among tech giants. You can ask: What does SpaceX look like without Elon Musk? What does Meta look like without Mark Zuckerberg? I think the same principle applies here, particularly in an emergency situation like this,” Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at the Eurasia Group, told Al Jazeera.

Musk came under scrutiny from the board at the electric vehicle maker as his attention was divided among a growing portfolio of businesses, which was a distraction from the company.

Musk’s increasingly public political activities with the administration of US President Donald Trump became a source of controversy for Tesla, with the company facing protests at its showrooms amid damage to its brand image and declining vehicle sales. In the first quarter of 2025, Tesla deliveries fell 13 percent year over year to their lowest level in nearly three years.

Ultimately, Tesla’s board opted not to remove him. However, his other company made changes to its governance structure that made it essentially impossible for the board to fire him when SpaceX prepared to go public earlier this year.

Musk was expected to retain approximately 82 percent of SpaceX’s total voting power after the IPO, despite selling shares to outside investors, a move that gave him control of who sits on the board, a role that is supposed to oversee the CEO. The Texas-based aerospace giant wrote into its charter that removal requires approval from holders of its special class of shares, and because Musk owns the majority of those shares, he can veto his own firing.

For Nvidia, Huang’s leadership often paid off. Nvidia invested heavily in graphics processing and helping build out data centre infrastructure amid a rapid expansion in the AI sector.

Nvidia has continued to make those kinds of investments. Just this week, the company agreed to purchase $10bn worth of shares in a private placement ahead of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO next week.

Nvidia’s management structure was heavily centred around Huang. He had dozens of executives reporting to him directly rather than operating within a more traditional hierarchical chain of command.

Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang could be removed by the 11-person board of directors “with or without cause”, as they hold a majority of votes. Unlike other tech giants, Huang does not have outsized control. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company and does not have majority voting power.

Nvidia’s structure is unique among major Silicon Valley companies.

Meta and Alphabet, for example, have special stock arrangements that give their founders more voting power than their actual ownership stakes would normally provide. As a result, founders like Zuckerberg can maintain control over who sits on the board, which can make it more difficult for shareholders to challenge leadership decisions.

This means that while Huang had enormous influence over Nvidia’s direction, he did not have the same formal voting control wielded by other major tech founders.

The company appointed Kress as its interim CEO. She previously served as Nvidia’s chief financial officer.

Historically, when a founder leaves, it hurts the direction of the company and can sway its competitive advantage in the market, and it has happened several times in corporate history.

In the 1980s, after a power struggle between Apple founder Steve Jobs and then CEO John Sculley, the company struggled for a decade. By 1997, the tech giant was on the brink of bankruptcy, with nearly $1bn in losses that year.

“When Apple’s founder Steve Jobs left the company for the first time, Apple experienced a major downturn, eventually prompting the board to invite him back,” Lu said.

When Jobs returned to the company, the Cupertino, California-based tech giant’s luck began to change and led to the launch of its most well-known products, including the iMac and the iPhone.

Starbucks faced a similar setback after founder Howard Schultz stepped down as CEO in 2000. He handed leadership to Orin Smith, the company’s then-president and chief operating officer.

The Seattle-based coffee shop chain continued to grow under Smith, but struggled after he retired in 2005 and was replaced by Jim Donald. Amid slowing sales and increased competition, Starbucks lost more than 80 percent of its value.

In January 2008, Schultz returned as CEO and launched a turnaround effort that included closing hundreds of underperforming locations.

However, founder-led companies are not necessarily destined for a downturn when their founders leave.

Jobs, who left the company in 1985, returned in 1997 and led its subsequent turnaround before handing the reins to former CEO Tim Cook in 2011. Under Cook, Apple continued to grow, briefly surpassing a $5 trillion market capitalisation in July 2026.

At Microsoft, Bill Gates stepped down as CEO in 2000, with Steve Ballmer succeeding him. After Ballmer retired in 2014, Satya Nadella took over.

Nadella shifted the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant’s focus towards cloud computing and enterprise software – a move that helped its market capitalisation grow from approximately $302bn in 2014 to $3.88 trillion in November 2026.

Nvidia faces another issue, and that is that much of the AI sector’s growth is pegged to its powerful chips.

OpenAI, which is eyeing an IPO, has up to $100bn worth of planned financial agreements with Nvidia. Nvidia has also agreed to invest $10bn in Dario Amodei-led Anthropic through a private placement tied to its planned US IPO, which could take place as early as next week.

articles.title: Man sells property and takes Rs 5.22 lakh in cash and remaining in bank account, faces income tax penalty for cash transaction; ITAT cancels it because tax officer applied wrong section
articles.summary: In cases of property deals, cash transactions are allowed up to a certain limit.
articles.body: In cases of property deals, cash transactions are allowed up to a certain limit. What if you sell a property and take a part in cash and the Income Tax Department imposes a penalty?In one case, the assessee faced a tax penalty but managed to get relief, but only on a technical ground. Read on to find out why the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) ruled in favour of the property seller.What the case is aboutA property owner sold it and accepted Rs 5.22 lakh in cash while the balance amount was received in his bank account. Income tax provisions prohibit the receipt of more than Rs 2 lakh in cash in such transactions.The Income Tax Assessing Officer (AO) in Berhampur received information from the property registrar's office in Jharsuguda that the man had sold a property and collected Rs 5.22 lakh in cash as part of the payment. The registered sale deed also mentioned the cash component.Following this information, the AO issued the man a notice under Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act and levied a penalty under Section 271DA.The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Cuttack, has granted relief to the man.Why did ITAT rule in favour of property seller?Appearing for the man before the ITAT Cuttack, his counsel argued that the AO had relied on Section 269SS to treat the cash received as sale consideration as a violation of income tax law.However, the counsel contended that Section 269ST, which came into effect from AY 2017-18, was the provision applicable to this particular violation.To substantiate his argument, the counsel referred to an earlier ITAT Cuttack ruling in the case of Arati Saraf (ITA No. 375/CTK/2023), dated May 13, 2024.He drew the tribunal’s attention to the ITAT Cuttack’s ruling in the Arati Saraf case, in which the tribunal had examined a similar issue.In that matter, the Assessing Officer had invoked Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act and imposed a penalty under Section 271D for cash received during the sale of immovable property.However, Sections 269ST and 271DA had been introduced to deal with violations involving cash transactions exceeding Rs 2 lakh.The counsel argued that the AO had failed to invoke the relevant provisions in this case, even though the transaction fell under Section 269ST.In its ruling in the Arati Saraf matter, the ITAT Cuttack had also explained the legislative intent behind the provision.The tribunal referred to the memorandum and notes on clauses accompanying the Finance Bill, 2015, which made it clear that the amendment was intended to curb the generation of black money in real estate transactions by prohibiting the acceptance of specified advances in cash.It observed that the term “specified sum” applied only to an “advance” receivable, while the expression “advance otherwise” meant that the advance could take any form.The tribunal further held in Arati Saraf’s case that the provision did not apply where no cash advance had been received and the cash payment was made at the time the sale deed was registered.Arati Saraf’s case fell into this category because, as admitted, the entire cash amount had been received in a single payment when the sale deed was executed. The ITAT Cuttack therefore concluded that Section 269SS had not been violated and had been wrongly invoked in that transaction.In this matter, the ITAT Cuttack relied on the reasoning in Arati Saraf and found that the facts clearly established that Section 269SS was not applicable to the transaction for which the AO had imposed a penalty under Section 271D.The tribunal observed: “This being so, respectfully following the decision of the coordinate bench of this Tribunal in the case of Arati Saraf as also in the case of Satyabrata Panda, as it is noticed that the AO has applied the provisions of Section 269SS in this case instead of applying the provisions of Section 269ST; therefore, the penalty levied under Section 271D stands cancelled.”Consequently, on October 5, 2026, the ITAT Cuttack ruled in the man’s favour and cancelled the penalty.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.summary: Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
articles.body: Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract. In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US. But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia, the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips. At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China. Also known as Huang Le, the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment. But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers. “Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.” But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable. On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls. “Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said. A billion-dollar business In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them. US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those. Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia. Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips. “If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.” Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba. In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said. Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year. “This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN. “It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said. Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations. In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing. Closing the loopholes The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia. Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue. However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well. They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.” Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted. Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment. Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. A growing number of chip smuggling cases has fueled calls for harsher legal enforcement outside the US as well. The Taiwanese government is seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong. “There’s going to have to be new standards that are going to have to be enforced around traceability and transparency,” Capri said. “This is really going to be the beginning of a major crackdown, and actually moving on to the next phase of export control enforcement.”

articles.title: From SpaceX's IPO to orbital data centers, execs say industry's future still in 'earliest innings'
articles.summary: SpaceX's (SPCX) blockbuster IPO this year put the space economy squarely on Wall Street's radar. The bigger question for investors now is where the next leg...
articles.body:
SpaceX's ( SPCX ) blockbuster IPO this year put the space economy squarely on Wall Street's radar. The bigger question for investors now is where the next leg of growth comes from.

That was the focus of "From Rockets to Revenue: Sizing Up the Space Economy," a panel at Yahoo Finance's Invest Conference earlier this week. Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ) CEO Jason Kim, Muon Space CEO Jonny Dyer, and Roundhill Investments ETF strategist Thomas DiFazio weighed in on launch economics, the next generation of satellites, defense, and data centers in orbit.

The SpaceX IPO marked space going mainstream. "The thing I take away from it is that space is now mainstream," said Dyer, a former SpaceX employee. For 60 years, space was "the domain of only big governments and defense," he said. Now, technology and infrastructure on Earth and in space are converging, and "we're just in the earliest innings."

DiFazio, whose firm runs the Roundhill Space & Technology ETF ( MARS ), called the offering's size and valuation "a really major endorsement" of the industry. He acknowledged the "emotional" fever pitch around the debut subsided as investors work out where the sector goes next.

The scale has changed dramatically. The late 1950s and early 1960s saw single-digit launches a year. Today there are hundreds, moving space "from what has been a government-led sector to what is now commercial-scale infrastructure," DiFazio said.

Launch demand still outstrips supply. DiFazio said launch providers are "not going anywhere," citing growing backlogs. Kim said customers are "just dying for more capacity."

Firefly is ramping up its small Alpha rocket, with six ship sets of Reaver engine chambers delivered in the fourth quarter alone. Flight 8 is preparing to launch, with flights 9 through 12 right behind it. Its medium-lift Eclipse rocket has logged more than 175 hot fires of its Miranda engine, totaling over 4,200 seconds.

Kim called Firefly's recent deal with AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) a "win-win." AST gets control of its launch schedule and economics by licensing Firefly's IP to build its own Miranda engines. Firefly gets a capital injection to accelerate Eclipse production. "The world needs Eclipse more than ever," Kim said.

Kim's broader pitch is to build a "railroad to the moon" with small- and medium-lift rockets, orbital transfer vehicles, and landers. Firefly won a $75 million JPL mission called Moonfall to carry drones to the moon, following its Blue Ghost lander's 14-day surface operation.
